paragraphs: The exploits of Diomedes, who keeps fighting even though Pandarus has wounded him—He kills Pandarus and wounds Aeneas—Aphrodite rescues Aeneas, but Diomedes wounds her too, and she hands him over to Apollo’s care and goes to Olympus, where her mother Dione tends her—Ares urges the Trojans on, and Aeneas, cured of his wound, returns to the fight—Athena and Hera help the Achaeans, and on the advice of Athena Diomedes wounds Ares, who goes back to Olympus to be cured.

Then Pallas Athena filled Diomedes, son of Tydeus, with courage, so that he would stand out above all the other Argives and win glory for himself. She made a stream of fire blaze from his shield and helmet, like the star that shines brightest in summer after bathing in the waters of Oceanus. She set that same fire burning on his head and shoulders, and told him to hurry into the thickest of the hurly-burly of the fight.

Among the Trojans there was a rich and honorable man named Dares, a priest of Hephaestus. He had two sons, Phegeus and Idaeus, both skilled in every kind of fighting. These two left the main body of the Trojans and went for Diomedes. They were in their chariot, and he was on foot. When they were close, Phegeus aimed first, but his spear passed over Diomedes’s left shoulder and missed him. Then Diomedes threw, and his spear did not fly in vain: it hit Phegeus on the chest near the nipple, and he fell from the chariot. Idaeus did not dare to stand over his brother’s body. He jumped down from the chariot and ran, and he would have shared his brother’s fate if Hephaestus had not saved him by wrapping him in a cloud of darkness, so that his old father would not be utterly crushed with grief. The son of Tydeus drove off with their horses and told his followers to take them to the ships. The Trojans were frightened when they saw the two sons of Dares, one running in terror and the other lying dead beside his chariot. Then Athena took Ares by the hand and said, “Ares, Ares, bane of men, blood-stained stormer of cities, why do we not leave the Trojans and Achaeans to fight it out, and see to which of them Zeus will grant the victory? Let us go away and so avoid his anger.”

With these words she led Ares out of the battle and sat him down on the steep banks of the Scamander. Then the Danaans pushed the Trojans back, and each of their chieftains killed his man. King Agamemnon was first: he threw mighty Odius, captain of the Halizoni, from his chariot. Odius was turning to run when Agamemnon’s spear caught him in the middle of the back. It struck between his shoulders and went right through his chest, and his armor clattered around him as he fell heavily to the ground.

Next Idomeneus killed Phaesus, son of Borus the Meonian, who had come from Varne. Phaesus was climbing into his chariot when mighty Idomeneus speared him in the right shoulder. He fell heavily from the car, and the darkness of death closed around him.

The squires of Idomeneus stripped Phaesus of his armor. Meanwhile Menelaus, son of Atreus, killed Scamandrius, the son of Strophius, a mighty huntsman and keen lover of the chase. Artemis herself had taught him to kill every kind of wild creature bred in the mountain forests. But neither she nor his famed skill with the bow could save him now. He was running away when the spear of Menelaus struck him in the back, between the shoulders, and went right through his chest. He fell headlong, and his armor clattered around him.

Then Meriones killed Phereclus, son of Tecton and grandson of Hermon, a man whose hands were skilled in every kind of cunning craftsmanship, because Pallas Athena had loved him dearly. He was the one who built the ships for Paris, the beginning of all the trouble, which brought evil on the Trojans and on Paris himself. He had paid no heed to the decrees of heaven. Meriones caught up with him as he ran, and struck him on the right buttock. The point of the spear went through the bone into the bladder. Phereclus cried out, fell forward on his knees, and death came over him.

Meges, too, killed Pedaeus, son of Antenor. Pedaeus was a bastard, but Theano had raised him like one of her own children, out of love for her husband. The son of Phyleus came up close and drove a spear into the back of his neck. It passed under his tongue and in among his teeth, so that he bit the cold bronze and fell dead in the dust.

Eurypylus, son of Euaemon, killed Hypsenor, the son of noble Dolopion. Hypsenor had been made priest of the river Scamander and was honored among the people like a god. Eurypylus chased him as he fled, struck him on the arm with his sword, and cut his strong hand off. The bloody hand fell to the ground, and the shades of death, with a fate no man can withstand, came over Hypsenor’s eyes.

So furiously the battle raged between them. As for the son of Tydeus, you could not tell whether he was fighting among the Achaeans or the Trojans. He swept across the plain like a winter torrent in full flood that has burst its banks. No dikes can hold it back, and no walls of fruitful vineyards can contain it when rain from heaven has swollen it. In a moment it comes tearing on and lays waste many a field that many a strong man’s hand has reclaimed. In the same way the son of Tydeus drove the dense ranks of the Trojans in rout, and many as they were, they dared not stand against his onslaught.

The son of Lycaon saw him sweeping across the plain and driving the Trojans in confusion before him. He aimed an arrow and hit him on the front of his cuirass, near the shoulder. The arrow went right through the metal and into the flesh, and the cuirass was covered with blood. The son of Lycaon shouted in triumph, “Trojan knights, come on! The bravest of the Achaeans is wounded, and he will not last much longer, if King Apollo was truly with me when I set out from Lycia to come here.”

So he boasted, but his arrow had not killed Diomedes. Diomedes pulled back and went to the chariot and horses of Sthenelus, the son of Capaneus. “Dear son of Capaneus,” he said, “come down from your chariot and pull the arrow out of my shoulder.”

Sthenelus jumped down from his chariot and drew the arrow from the wound, and blood came spouting out through the hole it had made in his shirt. Then Diomedes prayed: “Hear me, unwearying daughter of aegis-bearing Zeus. If you ever loved my father and stood by him in the thick of a fight, do the same for me now. Let me come within a spear’s throw of that man and kill him. He was too quick for me and has wounded me, and now he boasts that I will not see the light of the sun much longer.”

So he prayed, and Pallas Athena heard him. She made his limbs supple and quickened his hands and feet. Then she came close to him and said, “Do not be afraid, Diomedes, to fight the Trojans. I have put into your heart the spirit of your knightly father Tydeus. I have also lifted the veil from your eyes, so that you can tell gods from men. So if any other god comes here and offers you battle, do not fight him. But if Aphrodite, the daughter of Zeus, comes, strike her with your spear and wound her.”

After saying this Athena went away, and the son of Tydeus took his place again among the foremost fighters. He was three times as fierce as he had been before. He was like a lion that a mountain shepherd has wounded but not killed as it springs over the wall of a sheep-yard to attack the sheep. The shepherd has roused the beast to fury but cannot defend his flock, so he takes shelter in the buildings. The sheep, panic-stricken at being deserted, are smothered in heaps one on top of another, and the angry lion leaps out over the sheep-yard wall. That was how Diomedes went furiously about among the Trojans.

He killed Astynous and Hypeiron, shepherd of his people. He struck Astynous with a spear thrust above the nipple, and Hypeiron with a sword cut on the collarbone that severed his shoulder from his neck and back. He left both of them lying and went after Abas and Polyidus, sons of the old reader of dreams Eurydamas. They never came back for him to read them any more dreams, because mighty Diomedes made an end of them. Next he chased Xanthus and Thoon, the two sons of Phaenops. Both were very dear to their father, who was worn out with age and had no more sons to inherit his possessions. But Diomedes took both their lives and left their father grieving bitterly. He never saw them come home alive from the battle, and his kinsmen divided his wealth among themselves.

Next he met two sons of Priam, Echemmon and Chromius, riding in a single chariot. A lion will leap on the neck of a cow or heifer when the herd is grazing in a coppice, and he leapt on them in the same way. They fought back in vain. He threw both of them out of their chariot and took the armor off their bodies. Then he handed their horses to his comrades, to be led back to the ships.

Aeneas saw him making havoc among the ranks. He went through the fight, through the rain of spears, to look for Pandarus. When he found the brave son of Lycaon, he said, “Pandarus, where are your bow, your winged arrows and your renown as an archer now? No man here can rival you in that, and nobody in Lycia can beat you. Lift your hands to Zeus and send an arrow at this fellow who is going about so masterfully and has done such deadly work among the Trojans. He has killed many a brave man—unless he is some god who is angry with the Trojans about their sacrifices and, in his displeasure, has set his hand against them.”

The son of Lycaon answered, “Aeneas, I take him to be none other than the son of Tydeus. I know him by his shield, by the visor of his helmet and by his horses. He may be a god, but if he is the man I say he is, he is not making all this havoc without heaven’s help. Some god stands by his side, shrouded in a cloud of darkness, and that god turned my arrow aside when it had hit him. I have already shot at him and hit him on the right shoulder. My arrow went through the breast-piece of his cuirass, and I felt sure I had sent him hurrying to the world below. But it seems I have not killed him, so there must be a god who is angry with me. On top of that, I have neither horse nor chariot. In my father’s stables there are eleven excellent chariots, fresh from the builder and quite new, with cloths spread over them, and beside each one stands a pair of horses, champing barley and rye. My old father Lycaon urged me again and again, when I was at home and about to set out, to take chariots and horses with me so that I could lead the Trojans in battle. I would not listen to him. It would have been much better if I had. But I was thinking of the horses, which were used to eating their fill, and I was afraid they would go short of food in such a great gathering of men. So I left them at home and came on foot to Ilium, armed only with my bow and arrows. It seems these are of no use, for I have already hit two chieftains, the sons of Atreus and of Tydeus, and although I certainly drew blood, I have only made them more furious. I did wrong to take my bow down from its peg on the day I led my band of Trojans to Ilium in Hector’s service. If I ever get home again and see my native place, my wife and my great house, may someone cut my head off then and there if I do not break this bow and put it on a hot fire. That is the kind of tricks it plays on me.”

Aeneas answered, “Say no more. Things will not improve until the two of us go against this man with a chariot and horses and put him to the test of arms. Get into my chariot and see how skillfully the horses of Tros can race this way and that over the plain, in pursuit or in flight. If Zeus grants glory to the son of Tydeus again, they will carry us safely back to the city. So take the whip and reins while I stand on the car to fight. Or else you wait for this man’s attack, and I will look after the horses.”

“Aeneas,” replied the son of Lycaon, “take the reins and drive yourself. If we have to flee from the son of Tydeus, the horses will go better with their own driver. If they miss the sound of your voice when they expect it, they may take fright and refuse to carry us out of the fight. Then the son of Tydeus will kill both of us and take the horses. So drive them yourself, and I will meet him with my spear.”

They climbed into the chariot and drove at full speed toward the son of Tydeus. Sthenelus, son of Capaneus, saw them coming and said to Diomedes, “Diomedes, son of Tydeus, man after my own heart, I see two mighty heroes speeding toward you. One is a skilled archer, Pandarus son of Lycaon. The other is Aeneas, whose father is Anchises and whose mother is Aphrodite. Get into the chariot and let us retreat. I beg you, do not press so furiously forward, or you may get killed.”

Diomedes looked at him angrily and answered, “Do not talk of flight, for I will not listen. I come from a race that knows neither flight nor fear, and my limbs are not yet tired. I have no wish to mount the chariot. I will go against them just as I am. Pallas Athena tells me to be afraid of no man, and even if one of them escapes, their horses will not carry both back. I say more, and take my words to heart. If Athena sees fit to grant me the glory of killing both, stay here with your horses and tie the reins fast to the rim of the chariot. Then be sure to spring on Aeneas’s horses and drive them from the Trojan ranks to the Achaean. They come from the stock that great Zeus gave to Tros in payment for his son Ganymede, and they are the finest that live and move under the sun. King Anchises stole the breed by putting his mares to them without Laomedon’s knowledge, and they bore him six foals. Four are still in his stables, but he gave the other two to Aeneas. We shall win great glory if we can take them.”

So they talked, but the other two had now driven close, and the son of Lycaon spoke first. “Great and mighty son,” he said, “of noble Tydeus, my arrow failed to bring you down, so now I will try my spear.”

As he spoke he poised his spear and hurled it. It struck the shield of the son of Tydeus. The bronze point pierced it and went on until it reached the breastplate. The son of Lycaon shouted out, “You are hit clean through the belly. You will not last long, and the glory of the fight is mine.”
But Diomedes, quite undismayed, answered, “You missed, you did not hit. Before the two of you see the end of this, one or the other of you will glut tough-shielded Ares with his blood.”

With that he hurled his spear, and Athena guided it onto Pandarus’s nose, near the eye. It crashed in among his white teeth. The bronze point cut through the root of his tongue and came out under his chin. His glistening armor clattered around him as he fell heavily to the ground. The horses shied away in fear, and his life and strength were gone.
